defaults.label: On brief
defaults.description: Is the draft about what the brief asks, for the reader it names? Judged apart from how well it's written.

defaults.label: Argument
defaults.description: Is the main point clear, and does the draft make the case for it?

defaults.label: Evidence
defaults.description: Are the claims backed by sources, examples or figures that actually fit them?

defaults.label: Development
defaults.description: Is there enough on-topic material to earn the main point?

defaults.label: Straight talk
defaults.description: Free of padding, vague words, repetition and claims stated more strongly than shown.

defaults.label: Structure
defaults.description: Does each part follow from the last, with clear turns between them?

defaults.label: Rhythm
defaults.description: Do sentence lengths vary enough to keep the reader moving?

defaults.label: Voice
defaults.description: Does it sound like one writer, pitched at the reader the brief names?

defaults.label: Word choice
defaults.description: Precise, varied words rather than repeats, abstractions and jargon.

defaults.label: Paragraphs
defaults.description: A readable mix of short and long paragraphs, each doing one job.

defaults.label: Reader pull
defaults.description: Would the reader stay to the end? Follows the overall grade rather than being marked on its own.

moves.move: Reread who the brief is for and what it should do. Find the section that serves neither, then cut it or point it back.
Say your main point in one sentence near the top. Then check that each section supports it.
Pick your two shakiest claims and back each one with a source, an example or a number.
Find the point you move past fastest and give it one more paragraph: an example, a consequence, or an objection answered.
Swap claims about “always” and “everyone” for ones you can show. Cut the filler words.
Where the argument changes direction, add a break or a linking sentence. Cut a paragraph that repeats one before it.
Break one long sentence into two or three, and join two short ones.
Rewrite your first line in the tone you want, and let it set the pitch for the rest.
Swap three abstract words for concrete ones, and cut one piece of jargon per paragraph.
Split any paragraph longer than about six sentences, so each one does a single job.
Give the reader a reason to keep going in the first 100 words: a stake, or a question.
Make the one change that would lift this score most, then reread.
